lead: Bigger yacht, worse weather, a number or a decision wanted. Rope stretches or it does not, an anchor holds only along the seabed, and every load needs somewhere strong to go.

sections.title: Stretch, strength, and what a knot costs

head: Rope
Behaviour and use
rows: Stretches: snubbers, tow and dock lines. Stiff and faded is weak
1% stretch, slippery, melts near 150 °C: no snubber
Flexing and UV weaken it unseen: replace on age

blocks.p: A **splice** keeps about 90%, a bowline 60%, a tight turn over a thin pin less; divide what is left by a safety factor for the **safe working load**.

fig.title: Working load of a tow line
lines: 16 mm nylon: breaks at 6.0 t when new

list: Nylon: five tucks in an eye splice; a **long splice** keeps the diameter. Dyneema: knots slip, bury a long tapered tail.
Heavy warps: a seized **carrick bend** still unties; a bowline shakes loose in a surge. Sew whippings; coil right-hand lay clockwise; end-for-end a worn halyard.

fig.title: Doubled lines in a surge
lines: Line A 6 m, line B 12 m, both just taut
Stiffness ∝ 1 ÷ length: A is twice as stiff
A takes two-thirds of every snatch
Make doubled lines the same length

head: Seabed
What holds
rows: Roll-bar anchor: resets as she swings

blocks.p: The **gypsy** fits one chain standard; another jumps off under load. Lengthen the rode with 8-plait nylon spliced into the last link. Size chain for the whole load, worn: a **snubber** spares the windlass, not the chain.
Lower **under power** in deep water: free-falling chain outruns the brake. The windlass lifts only what hangs off the bottom. Lash the bitter end where you can cut it.

sections.title: Enough rode, enough room, and a watch
refs: Anchoring — scope by depth and weather
Anchoring — at night on a strange coast

blocks.p: **Scope** is measured from the bow roller: depth plus its height, times the ratio, 7:1 for a gale on chain and rope. Heavier chain needs less.

fig.title: Room to swing
lines: Radius = chain along the bottom + boat
60 m of chain, roller 12 m above the seabed
Boats lying differently: add both radii

blocks.p: Log a **radar range and bearing** every 15 minutes and set the alarm. An arc on the plotter is swinging, a straight line downwind dragging. Leave an open roadstead before an onshore gale; a strange bay at night: radar, sounder, a charted contour.

Against **sheering**: a riding sail aft on a ketch, a second anchor under foot on a high-bowed motor yacht. The **kedge** goes out in the tender, warp paid out as you go; aground on a lee bank, lay it to windward now.

sections.title: A V for a gale, a line for a stream
refs: Anchoring — two anchors in a river

blocks.p: For a gale that will veer, lay both anchors ahead in a **V** across the shift, so each takes its share.

fig.note: Gale SW 8, veering W: an anchor towards each

blocks.p: In a reversing stream lay a **Bahamian moor**: two anchors in line with it, the yacht between. Let go up-stream, drop back twice the scope, let go again, heave back to the middle. A cross wind pushes her sideways until both legs are taut.

fig.note: A swivel joins the rodes · weigh the slack anchor first

sections.title: Springs, screws and the stream
refs: Boat handling — prop walk and wind
Twin screws — docking in a stream

fig.note: Astern on the spring, fender aft: the bow swings out

blocks.p: **Twin screws**: one ahead, one astern, the stern swings towards the engine going ahead; thruster the same way and she walks sideways. One engine astern alone throws the stern away from it: outward-turning, offset and prop walk add up. A right-handed propeller kicks the stern to port astern: get sternway on early.

fig.note: Starboard ahead, port astern, thruster to starboard

head: Berth
What works
rows: Both engines ahead, bow angled in: it ferries her over
Pass the berth, back up against it
Up-tide pile first; fender board in a swell
Slack in long springs: 15 m needs 0.8 m for 5 m
Largest inside; outer boats cast off to let you out

fig.title: Stern-to in a gusty crosswind
lines: Gusts 26 kn: load ≈ V² ÷ 60 kgf per m²
Anchor upwind, snub the chain: it holds the bow

blocks.p: Plan for the gust; the thruster is for short bursts. **Crossed stern lines** check a sideways swing; where lazy lines lie, your anchor fouls the ground chains.

sections.title: A long, elastic line and a slow tow
refs: Towing — being towed by a ship
Towing — being towed by a larger vessel

head: Decide
Rule of thumb
rows: One wave length, 1.56 × T²: 8 s, 100 m
⅔ of hull speed 1.34 × √LWL ft: LWL 10 m, 5.1 kn
Pull ÷ 2 cos half-angle: 1.6 t at 90°, 1.1 t

blocks.p: Agree channel, speed and signals first. Make fast with turns round a strong point you can ease or cut; a ship's tow: spread the pull over mast foot and both bow cleats. **Chafe** parts tows; the spring is nylon's stretch, not a weight on the line.

fig.title: Night orders for the tow
lines: Watch aft on the line, knife to hand
Chafe and VHF check every hour
Tow steers in our wake; drogue if she sheers
Line parts: engines neutral, recover it
Before the bar: shorten up, then alongside

blocks.p: **Length of tow**: your stern to the tow's stern. Over 200 m: three masthead lights, not two, and diamonds by day. No towing lights? Light the towline (Rule 24(i)).
Never lie **a-hull**: beam-on, a breaking crest can roll her. Drift times hours of gale must fit your sea room.

head: Tactic
How
rows: Main eased, helm to leeward, 50° off the wind; slow
Drogue on a bridle to both quarters, 1.5 wave lengths; fast
Parachute from the bow on long nylon; least drift; trip line

fig.note: Hove-to, 50° off the wind. Forereaching? Ease the main

blocks.p: The **trysail** has its own track and two sheets to the quarters, led before hoisting; a forward lead tightens the leech. The **storm jib** hanks to an inner forestay on a tack pennant; try both in harbour.

fig.title: Can she run with the seas?
lines: She cannot keep up: slow down,

blocks.p: A motor yacht cannot heave to: she jogs at displacement speed, seas fine on the bow, and running lets faster waves pass, tabs up. A lowered **trim tab** lifts its own side; a burst ahead on the engine she yaws towards checks her.
